summary: For ages 6-7, with adult prompting, children move from showing a method to EXPLAINING and beginning to JUSTIFY it — using drawings, number sentences, or words to say not just what they did but WHY the answer is right. The characteristic gap is between convincing (confident but with an incomplete chain, 'I reckon it's right') and justifying (a correct, complete because-chain). Teaching supplies logical connectives and sentence stems, uses alternative-method agreement as a form of justification, and treats finding and explaining errors in worked examples as reasoning practice.
misconceptions: Confident assertion ('I reckon it's right') offered as justification, with an incomplete or incoherent chain (convincing mistaken for justifying)
Describing the method but stopping short of saying WHY it gives the right answer unless heavily prompted
Spotting that a worked example is wrong but being unable to explain the flaw
Treating 'justify' as 'do the sum again' rather than giving a reason

activities.title: The 'convince me' partner
steps: Pose the child a within-20 calculation (e.g. 8 + 5) and ask them to explain HOW they worked it out.
Then ask 'why does that work?' and 'how do you know it's right?' — not just 'what did you do?'.
When the child stalls or only asserts ('I just know', 'I reckon it's right'), hand over a sentence stem: 'Start with because…' and prompt for the missing link.
Have the child upgrade a confident hunch into a chain, e.g. 'because 5 is 2 and 3, and 8 and 2 make 10, so 10 and 3 more is 13'.
Ask the child to show the same calculation a different way and check whether it also gives the answer ('the other way also gives 13 — what does that tell us?').
Present a worked example containing a slip (e.g. a number bond that doesn't actually make ten) and ask 'Is this right? How can you tell?' — pushing for WHICH step is wrong and WHY.
activities.insight: A confident answer is not the same as a justification; a reason that works can be built by linking steps with 'because' and 'so', and an alternative method that agrees is supporting evidence that backs up the reason, though it does not replace explaining why.

activities.title: Build an explanation you can test
steps: Give the child step cards (number sentences / method steps) and connective tiles ('because', 'so', 'therefore') to arrange into an argument chain for why a calculation is right.
Have the child read the assembled chain aloud to check it actually hangs together and establishes the claim.
Check the answer a second way (an alternative method) and compare — do the two routes agree?
In an error-spotting task, give a worked example and have the child point to the wrong step AND say why it is wrong.
Keep drawings and number sentences as the backbone of the explanation throughout.
activities.insight: Justification is something you assemble and test, not just a confident feeling: steps linked with connectives form a chain; a second method checks whether the answer agrees, and checking each step tests whether the chain really holds.

activities.title: Model a complete because-chain (scaffold)
steps: Show a justified worked example where each step is paired with its 'because' reason, e.g. reveal one step at a time so the child sees what a full chain looks like.
After viewing, ask the child to re-tell the chain in their own words, then produce one for a fresh calculation themselves.
activities.insight: A worked justification shows the TARGET: every step has a reason, and the reasons connect to establish the answer.

activities.title: Critique items: real reason or just saying it's right? (complement)
steps: Present short 'find the error' items where the child selects the faulty step in a worked example, then says why it is faulty.
Present 'which is a proper reason vs just saying it's right?' items where the child picks the genuine justification over a confident restatement.
Use an open discussion counterexample (child must explain, not just pick): 'Someone got the right answer with a method that only works because these numbers are small — is their reasoning good?'
activities.insight: Recognising the difference between a reason and a confident assertion, and between good reasoning and a lucky right answer, may help a child see what a proper justification needs; recognising a good reason does not by itself produce one, so these items complement — not replace — the construction tasks.

checkQuestion: Pose a calculation such as 8 + 5. Ask: 'Explain how you'd work it out — and why is your answer right? Can you show it a different way to check?' Then show a worked example with an error (e.g. a bond that doesn't make ten) and ask: 'Is this right? How do you know?' Discuss the reasoning; do not mark a number.
checkAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for a child who explains the method AND gives a reason it works ('because 8 and 2 make 10, then 3 more is 13'), uses an alternative method as confirmation, and, shown the flawed example, says it is wrong and points to WHY. A complete because-chain and the ability to explain an error are the targets, not the arithmetic.
